title: Granular output contracts and client call flow - PRD notes
content:
Purpose

Working sketch for a minimal-surface PRD that focuses on: (1) making incremental/stepwise output deterministic for clients, (2) a low-friction tool-invocation handshake that works over streaming and non-streaming transport, and (3) an SDK layer that surfaces a small set of clear primitives for backpressure, commit semantics, and typed responses. This is intentionally practical — try small API changes first that unlock better client ergonomics without large runtime rewrites.

Context and problem statements
- Many of our customers build orchestration layers where partial model outputs are used to invoke downstream tools. Current streaming primitives are too free-form: clients cannot reliably know when an interim token sequence is intended as a final callable payload vs. fluff.
- SDKs try to hide streaming complexity but don't expose commit/retract primitives, forcing awkward hacks and fragile heuristics.
- Tool-handshake behavior is duplicated across apps: our platform should provide a concise, predictable contract so developers don't re-implement fallbacks.

Goals (measurable)
- Reduce client-side parsing errors for tool invocation payloads by 60% for pilot customers within 3 months of beta.
- Provide SDK primitive that reduces application code complexity (lines of code) for common tool-calls by 30% in sample apps.
- Ensure no-regression in latency P50/P90 when enabling incremental commits on hosted endpoints (+/- 5%).

Proposed surface (high level)
1) Output frames and lifecycle tags - Streaming responses are composed of discrete "frames". Each frame carries a lifecycle tag: draft | candidate | committed | retracted.
- Draft: ephemeral tokens that can be superseded without action. Candidate: flagged as a possible callable payload. Committed: final and durable (non-retractable). Retracted: explicit server retract.
- Clients can subscribe to specific lifecycle transitions (e.g., onCandidate, onCommit).

2) Soft-commit API attribute (request side)
- param: step_commit_mode = [automatic, client_ack, server_commit_only]
- automatic: server makes best-effort commits when confident. client_ack: server emits candidate frames and waits for client ack to commit. server_commit_only: legacy behavior, only server decisions create commits.

3) Tool invocation handshake (protocol sketch)
- 3-way flow for client_ack mode: server -> candidate (frame with typed contract) -> client -> ack(payloadId, intent=invoke|buffer) -> server -> commit or wait for edits.
- Typed contract: candidate frames include a schema hint (json-schema id) and a confidence score. Tool routing uses the schema id to validate and map to tool adapters.

4) SDK primitives (JS + Python surface ideas)
- session = hostedApi.startCall(options)
- session.on('candidate', (frame) => { /* lightweight validation */ })
- session.ack(frameId, {intent: 'invoke'|'buffer'})
- session.commit(frameId) // optional for client-initiated commit
- session.on('commit', (frame) => { /* durable result */ })
- session.on('retract', (frameId, reason))
- fallback: session.cancel() / session.flushToNonStreaming()

5) Backpressure and offline handling
- SDK exposes preferred buffer limit (soft) and an explicit flush API.
- If network conditions degrade, SDK can switch to a reliability-first non-streaming call (flushToNonStreaming) preserving the last candidate. This is important for mobile and flaky edge environments.

6) Telemetry and observability signals
- emit events: candidate_emitted, client_ack, server_commit, retraction, commit_latency_ms, candidate_to_commit_delta.
- tie candidate->commit chains to a trace id for per-request reconstruction in Console.

7) Security and validation
- Candidate frames that claim a typed contract must be validated against a server-side white-list of approved schemas for the customer (prevents clients from accidentally invoking arbitrary adapters).

Implementation plan (iterative)
- Phase 0 (spike, 2 weeks): implement frame lifecycle tags in a non-invasive streaming header. No changes to storage/retention; purely wire-level. Build a toy JS SDK wrapper to validate patterns.
- Phase 1 (8 weeks): add client_ack path + ack RPC. Add candidate telemetry and trace headers. Ship SDK primitives in beta.
- Phase 2 (8–12 weeks): server-side schema registry and tool-mapping integration. Add automatic commit heuristics and rollback behavior.

Compatibility, fallbacks, and error modes
- Non-upgraded clients receive standard tokens (no lifecycle tags). Servers must fall back to server_commit_only for old clients.
- If client_ack is requested but ack not received in X seconds, server may auto-commit based on policy or retract candidate.
- Retracted candidates emit explicit reasons (policy, validation-fail, low-confidence).

Open questions and tradeoffs
- Should commit be a true durable object in our storage (versioned) or only implied in the stream? Durable commits enable better replay and audit but increase storage semantics.
- How heavy should schema validation be? We can start with lightweight JSON-schema matching and incrementally add stronger validation.
- UX: exposing lifecycle tags increases surface area for users who "just want text". SDKs must keep the default path simple (autocommit) and surface advanced modes opt-in.

Pilot plan and success criteria
- Identify 2 internal pilot teams (Console automation + Solutions Eng) to exercise ack-mode. Build 3 sample adapters (search, calendar, ticket-create) and measure false-invoke rate.
- Success: pilot reduces false-invoke incidents by at least 50% and SDK adoption in pilot teams within 6 weeks.

Notes to self / next steps
- Sync with runtime on minimal wire format and trace header names (ask Ethan).
- Proto sample for candidate frame to include: id, tokensPreview (short), schemaId, score, estimatedCostMs.
- Draft small example app that uses session.ack to perform safe calendar creation.

This doc is intentionally a sketch. Priority is to ship a small-surface API that improves developer confidence around tool invocation and reduces ad-hoc parsing. Keep things opt-in and shield the majority of customers from extra complexity by sensible defaults.
